title: stream-safe response builders and typed hydration for python sdk
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Create a set of stream-safe response builders and typed hydration helpers for the Python SDK that make it ergonomic to consume chunked/streamed model outputs as strongly-typed Python records while preserving backwards compatibility with existing untyped streaming APIs. Focus areas: incremental JSON decoding, partial-object assembly, robust retry/interruption semantics, and user-facing ergonomics for async and sync streams.
background: Current Python SDK streaming helpers expose raw event chunks and require callers to stitch partial JSON payloads themselves or rely on ad-hoc helper code in customer repos. This causes duplicated logic, subtle bugs when messages are split across TCP frames, and makes retries/cancellation awkward for typed response consumers. Several internal repos have implemented hacks to reassemble tokens or do repeated json.loads which is fragile under partial chunks. We need a first-class, well-tested abstraction that provides: (1) low-overhead incremental parsing, (2) a mapping layer to typed models (dataclasses or pydantic), and (3) clear semantics around retrying and restarting streams without leaking half-constructed objects.
acceptance_criteria: A single public API in the Python SDK (ModelResponseBuilder) that accepts an async generator of bytes/strings and yields typed Python objects (dataclass or pydantic) for each complete logical message.

Streaming parser handles JSON objects split across arbitrary chunk boundaries, escape sequences, and array-wrapped event streams used by hosted API; unit tests cover all split-along-byte-boundary cases.
Backwards compatibility: existing streaming iterator that yields raw chunks remains available and interoperates with the new builder; major version bump avoided.
Retry semantics: consumers can call .retry_from_checkpoint() to re-open a stream from the last confirmed message; no duplicate typed objects are emitted on graceful retries.
Comprehensive benchmarks demonstrating <=10% added latency for typed hydration over raw stream for typical 1-2KB messages and <=2x memory overhead compared to naive in-memory reassembly.
Detailed migration guide and examples (sync/async) added to SDK docs and example repository with a mini tutorial showing function-calling and structured output use-cases.
At least two partner teams (console and dedicated) validate the API in a short integration spike and sign off on ergonomics.
All new code covered by unit and integration tests and approved in a pull request with CI green (including flakiness checks for streaming tests).
Telemetry: add high-level telemetry events for parse errors and recoveries (opt-outable) so we can surface customer mis-parsing without shipping PII.
implementation_plan: Spike: implement an incremental JSON tokenizer based on Python's built-in json.scanner to avoid full-buffer json.loads (done, bench results attached)
Design public API: ModelResponseBuilder (context manager) + StreamingTypedIterator -> yields typed models or raises StructuredParseError for unrecoverable payload corruption
Provide two mapping backends: lightweight dataclass mapper (no runtime deps) and optional pydantic mapper (for strict validation). Provide a factory to select mapper at runtime.
Implement checkpointing: emit wall-clock and logical sequence id per typed object; persist minimal checkpoint token for retrying streams.
Edge cases: support array-wrapped streams, server-sent events format, and function-call structured outputs wrapped as nested objects.
Build migration helpers: from_raw_stream(generator) -> ModelResponseBuilder for easy adoption.
Add end-to-end integration tests using a local test server that intentionally splits JSON across random chunk sizes and injects transient 5xx to validate retry behavior.

Docs & examples: add a tutorials/sdk/streaming-typed-response.md plus a Jupyter example in examples/python/ demonstrating both sync and async usage, plus a small notebook for debugging partial chunks.
Rollout: release as a feature-flagged opt-in in python-sdk-2.4.0-beta, collect telemetry, then enable by default in 2.4.1 upon partner sign-off.
testing_plan: Unit tests for incremental tokenizer with fuzzing harness that replays 10k randomized chunk splits of representative payloads.
Property tests verifying that hydration(dataclass) == hydration(pydantic) for canonical payloads (ignoring minor type coercion differences).
Integration test that simulates network reconnect where the server replays a prefix and a checkpoint is used to avoid duplicates.
Performance tests measuring per-message latency and peak memory under a synthetic workload; CI will run microbenchmarks on ubuntu-latest with x86 runners.
Manual QA with two partner teams: console ingest of streaming chat, and dedicated capacity customer simulation for long-lived streams.
rollout_plan: Publish alpha beta to internal package index and request console + dedicated teams to test for 1 week
Collect telemetry and bug reports; fix high-priority parsing bugs; iterate on ergonomics based on feedback
Publish migration guide and code samples in SDK docs site; create a short video walking through migration
Ship stable release in python-sdk-2.4.1 with gradual rollout and monitor parse_error_rate and customer complaints for 2 weeks
Post-release: schedule follow-up to add TypeScript parity plan and create GH issue for cross-SDK design notes.
notes: Trade-offs considered: strict validation via pydantic provides better developer UX but adds runtime overhead and dependency surface; default will use dataclass mapper with an opt-in pydantic validator.
We considered shipping a streaming JSON-RPC layer but deferred to keep scope focused on typed message hydration and retry semantics.
Existing experimental code in infra/team-utils demonstrates checkpoint token layout; we will reuse token schema to avoid cross-service incompatibility.

Spike benchmark: incremental parser reduced peak memory by ~40% compared to naive buffering and improved median parse latency by 2.1x for our microbench payloads. Full benchmark is linked in related_docs.
